item.title: What is Grief? What to Expect in Each of the Stages of Grief and Loss
item.description:
We all have many different life experiences that make us unique. However, if we live long enough, grief is a shared experience many of us carry. Grief can be described as a response to loss. This usually involves the death of someone, but it can also include other losses such as divorce, loss of a home or job, or loss of health or independence.

Grief is normal and healthy

Grief is a normal and healthy response to loss. We might have grown up with the idea that grieving is abnormal and unhealthy (real men don’t cry), but this just isn’t true. God designed us to love and care deeply, and the response to losing those we love is grief.

Not only is it normal, but it’s also healthy. When we refuse to grieve, we actually cause ourselves harm. It’s like a balloon. We can only stuff so much air into a balloon before it pops. We are like that with our emotions. We can only “stuff” our feelings so much before we pop, too.

We might explode in anger, experience depression, or even experience physical symptoms such as stomach problems or headaches. Also, unresolved grief can build upon itself when we experience the next grief. When we choose to sweep things under the rug, we are just causing ourselves more work and agony the next time we experience loss.

When we grieve, we not only grieve the loss of the person, but we mourn the loss of the roles, dreams, nuances, and routines that went along with our relationship with them. These are called secondary losses. Roles include parts the loved one played that will possibly need to be passed on to others. Some examples of this are the “fun one”, tech guy, party planner, banker, cook, etc.

We experience a loss of dreams and expectations, such as the deceased person not being able to be there when grandchildren are born. More subtle things include the way a person smells, physical touch such as sleeping in the same bed, etc. There are also many changes in routine when we lose someone. This might include having Thanksgiving at someone else’s house or changing from a couple’s Sunday school class to a women’s or men’s class.

Everyone grieves differently. This is based on many factors such as personality, type of death, our relationship with them, support systems, etc. For instance, an individual would normally grieve the peaceful passing of their ninety-year-old grandmother differently than their child suddenly being killed in a car accident.

The type of death and circumstances surrounding it often have a major impact. Sometimes a good relationship with the deceased makes their death harder, but a rocky, estranged relationship can also make grieving difficult.

The Five Stages Grieving Model

One common grief model puts typical grieving into five stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. Let’s look at what we might expect from each stage.

Denial

Denial usually happens when we first learn about the loss. It can include shock, numbness, confusion, and fear. Our bodies and minds cannot process the news we have just received, and it is hard to believe what has happened. It can be a protective coping mechanism that helps us get through those first few weeks. It helps us be able to plan funerals and make lots of hard decisions.

Often people will wake up from sleep and wonder if the loss really happened or if it was just a dream. It might cause us to walk into that person’s house and briefly look for them or call them, forgetting that they aren’t there to answer. Sometimes people are concerned that they don’t have much emotion in the beginning. All of these are common in the first stage.

Anger

Anger is common in the grieving process and can be directed at many different people. We might be angry with ourselves for not doing something differently or spending enough time with them. We might be angry with a doctor or the driver who caused a car accident. We might be angry with God for allowing this terrible thing to happen. We might even be angry with the deceased for not taking better care of themself or for how they treated us.

Sometimes we’re angry because we had such a good relationship with them, and sometimes we’re angry because it was a traumatic or difficult relationship. Anger is often described as a secondary emotion, meaning we’re never “just angry.” We experience anger because of some other emotion such as pain, embarrassment, or guilt. We experience many varied emotions when we grieve, and they often come out as anger.

Bargaining

This takes place when we have “if only” thinking. “If only we didn’t go on vacation.” “If only we had seen the doctor sooner.” We use magical thinking to try to undo something that happened. We often experience guilt in this phase. We blame ourselves for the death, thinking somehow we could have prevented it.

We wish we had spent more time or said certain things. We spend lots of time longing for the person to come back and grasp at anything to try to undo what has happened. We know logically this is futile, but it is a natural part of grief.

Depression

This can take many forms. Of course we feel sad, but it usually goes deeper than that. We might experience physical symptoms such as headaches, pain, or stomach problems. We might not be able to sleep or sleep too much. We might not enjoy doing things that used to bring us joy. Difficulty concentrating and making decisions is also difficult during this phase. We can feel like we’re in a fog, or our brain just won’t work right.

Isolation from others is often common. Part of us knows we should and need to get out and be around friends, but we just don’t want to. Sometimes it’s because we feel sad, and sometimes it’s how we perceive others at this time. We might be angry that people didn’t reach out to us in the way or as frequently as we wanted. Sometimes we are aggravated that people won’t leave us alone.

People often don’t know how to act around the grieving person or what to say to them. They often say foolish and unintentionally hurtful things. “They’re in a better place.” “You should be thankful your dad lived that long.” Others are uncomfortable and feel the need to fill the silence with ill-thought-out words.

This hurts and frustrates us and makes us feel like others just don’t understand. Sometimes they avoid the grieving person or avoid the elephant in the room because they don’t know what to say or do. All of these can cause isolation and hurt. It’s also easy to have irrational thinking and be oversensitive during this time.

Acceptance

Acceptance is the final stage of grief. It is the opposite of bargaining or longing for what was lost. We finally accept the reality that our loved one is no longer here. While we never truly get over the loss, we learn to live with it. It becomes our new normal and is a sense of finality.

Often, those who have moved on to the acceptance phase of grief desire to give back to others. It helps them make sense of the loss by turning it into something good. This can include giving money in the person’s name for a cause, leading a grief group, or bringing a meal to a person who has just experienced loss.

Often people want to know how long the grieving process lasts. Unfortunately, there is no time limit or date on the calendar when it will be over. Some experts say grief lasts about two years, but that can depend on a lot of factors. The first year will be hard because we have to experience all the “firsts”: first Christmas, first birthday, and the anniversary of their death. These are often hard days for several years.

Next Steps

Grieving is one of the hardest events we can experience in life. There isn’t a pill to take or a procedure to hurry it up. We have to give ourselves time and permission to grieve. Grief takes time, but it also takes work.

If you feel you are struggling with your grief, don’t go it alone. Talk to a counselor or grief group to walk with you through this difficult time. They can give you a safe place to express your thoughts, memories, and emotions and help you work through this painful process.

item.title: The Roles of Mind, Self, and Brain in Healing Depression: Learning to Stay Out of the River of Our Negative Cognitions
item.description:
Depression occurs when stressful life events influence the brain. These events create more negative thoughts and feelings and more distortion in the way the brain processes information. To understand this process is it is important to realize that the human brain consists of three distinct components which have a role in the management of depression.

Three Components of Depression Management

The first component, which we will identify, is the mind, located in the anterior cingulate gyrus. The mind is the stream or river of consciousness through which flow thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. It is not the source of the content of the river; it is a conduit for processing the content.

The second component is the Self, located in the prefrontal cortex, on the bank of the mind or river of consciousness. This component is our sense of “I”, the internal executor of the brain, and in a real sense, this is where our soul resides, called our “heart” in the Scriptures.

The Self could observe the thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations which flow through the mind and process them. The Self observes the contents of the river, but they are not the same as the mind.

Just because a thought enters the river, it doesn’t mean you have to believe it – the Self determines the validity of the contents of the river. The limbic system of the brain is the source of the contents of the river – thoughts, images, feelings, and sensations. Remember, the brain is not the same component as the mind.

How the Brain Processes Information

The brain produces the stream of thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations by processing information from:

  • The real world
  • Your body and senses, including your gut
  • By recalling past packages of thoughts, feelings, beliefs, and motor/action plans or schemas that make sense of our experiences

For example, you see a plant while on a hike, and you’ve never seen one like it before. It might be a green leafy plant, but you’ve never seen this kind before. What is it? The automatic systems in your brain take over and process this real-world information with the anxiety you are feeling in your body and gut, as you are concerned this might actually be poison ivy, because you have heard there might be some around.

The brain then starts recalling things from your past. This plant has three leaves like the one you touched when you were a kid, so it sends anxiety and danger signals down the river. But these automatic functions only control 80% of your brain. The other 5-20 % come from the Self. So, you have some executor options. You can become overwhelmed by what the brain is sending, believe it, and jump in the river, or you can analyze and appraise.

You can say things like, yes, there might be poison ivy plants around, but they do not have leaves like the one I saw as a kid. Yes, poison ivy can cause problems, but didn’t that plant hurt me when I was a kid because I plucked it up? Have any of my friends had a problem with poison ivy on this trail?

The Brain and the Self

The brain is an organ, just like the gut or the heart. Sometimes it cooperates fully with the rest of the body, and sometimes it doesn’t. If you allow negative things into your brain, i.e., pornography, violent video games or movies, abuse, it will react negatively. You are not your brain, but you can change your brain.

Negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations sent into the river by the brain are observed by the Self, which is safely located on the bank in the real world, where it can reappraise after stepping back and seeing the situation clearly.

The problem develops when the Self becomes entangled in the river by ruminating on the thoughts and feelings it encounters there. You (Self) become the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations. This rumination results in a new reality. The Self, who is stuck in the river, creates a new thought: “My brain is telling me this, so it must be true!”

The result of this new reality is an overwhelming sense of sadness, lack of motivation, and loss of interest in things we formerly enjoyed. The Self is stuck in negative thoughts. One of the consequences of the Self being stuck in the river is that the prefrontal cortex is turned off and is not working as designed. The solution to the problem lies in learning to redirect attention to the real world through mindfulness techniques and cognitive restructuring.

Mindfulness

Mindfulness is keeping our thoughts in the present, where it is safe, and not in the past, which is dominated by “If onlys”, or the future, which is dominated by “What ifs.” Cognitive restructuring is challenging the validity and logic of the negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, using the logical prefrontal cortex where the Self resides.

The safest place to direct attention is to the real world, not the river. If we fall into the river, we drown in depression. So, the question you need to ask yourself is, “Is there anything happening right here, right now in this room with which you cannot deal or handle?”

Healing depression focuses on climbing out of the river by remembering the scriptural admonition to claim the promise of Philippians 4:7, and receive the peace of God, which the Apostle Paul states, “…Surpasses all understanding, and will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Phil. 4:7 ESV).

If we can learn not to live in the past or worry about the future, but instead to learn from the past and apply the lessons learned, we can face the future assured of the strength of the Lord to guide us. And in the process, we allow the Self to resume the executor role of the brain as God designed it, and we stay grounded in the present in the real world.

Research has shown that the Brain has the capacity to stay in the present for 4-7 seconds before it starts to wander to the past or future. Consequently, we need to empower the Self, steal that attention away from the brain, and mindfully bring it back to the present.

We accomplish this with in-the-moment coping skills, such as diaphragmatic breathing, mindfulness techniques that activate prefrontal cortex activity, and challenging the validity and logic of negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations.

Challenging Negative Thoughts

We can systematically challenge each negative thought, each negative feeling, each troubling image, and each sensation by identifying what percentage they are true. At first, we might think they are 90-100% true, and that’s what keeps us in the river. But the Self, which is watching from the riverbank, can see that the reality is that the percentage is much, much lower. A common example is “I can never do anything right!” and it is believed 100%.

But hearing the Self challenge the statement with the logic that no one is always wrong, and everyone does some things right, lowers the percentage substantially and starts on the path to healing. Allowing the Self to put the negatives on trial, and asking, “What is the evidence that I should believe this?”, is another effective way to climb out of the river.

In conclusion, don’t forget that living in the “If onlys” of the past and the “What ifs” of the future will cause the brain to convince us that there is no hope. When we get the Self and the prefrontal cortex involved in the challenging process, we can claim the promise that healing and peace are only a prayer away!

So, if you feel you are drowning in the river of your negative thoughts, feelings, images, and sensations, please know there is hope through a therapist who understands the healing process. Please check our website and make an appointment today. Peace awaits.

item.title: What is Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?
item.description:
We have all seen it before – a social media friend posts a picture of their perfectly color-coded closet. Their pantry is organized into matching containers. Every towel is folded exactly the same way. The caption reads: “#OCD.”

Or maybe you’ve seen someone look at a crooked picture frame or a stack of papers that isn’t perfectly straight and joke, “My OCD is going so crazy right now.” Most of us have laughed, nodded, or kept scrolling without thinking much about it.

But what if OCD is actually something completely different? What if the person silently battling Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder has a messy closet, an overflowing laundry basket, and a mind that never gives them a moment of peace?

The truth is that OCD has little to do with being neat, organized, or particular. It is a disorder driven by fear. It is a disorder built on uncertainty. And for those living with it, it can feel like you are battling a monster on steroids every single day.

Why OCD Thoughts Cause So Much Distress

One of the most difficult parts of OCD is that people often mistake intrusive thoughts for who they are.

An intrusive thought is exactly what it sounds like: an unwanted thought, image, or urge that repeatedly barges into your mind without your permission. These thoughts are distressing because they are the exact thoughts you do not want to have. If you could snap your fingers and make them disappear forever, you would.

Ironically, the harder you try to force them away, argue with them, or prove they are not true, the longer they tend to stick around. This is one of the reasons OCD is so exhausting. These types of thoughts are often referred to as “sticky thoughts” (also referred to as obsessions).

Everyone experiences random intrusive thoughts from time to time. A person who isn’t battling OCD may briefly notice the thought and move on with their day. Their brain simply lets it pass.

But someone dealing with OCD tends to get stuck. The thought lingers, replaying over and over. It may stay for hours or even days, demanding attention and creating tremendous anxiety. The brain becomes convinced that the thought must mean something important simply because it won’t leave.

People might think:

“What if I secretly want this?”
“What if this thought means something about me?”
“What if God is trying to tell me something?”
“What if everyone else is safe except me?”

However, the opposite is usually true. OCD likes to attack what matters most to us. A loving mother may develop terrifying thoughts about accidentally harming her child. A devoted Christian might become consumed with fears that they have committed an unforgivable sin or will in the future.

A compassionate person may become terrified that they could harm someone else, or even themselves, despite desperately not wanting to. Someone who deeply values honesty becomes trapped wondering if they lied without realizing it.

Deep down, people battling with OCD might even recognize that these thoughts are attacking the values they hold most dear. If a thought fills you with fear because it goes completely against who you are and what you believe, that is often evidence that it is not something you actually want to do. OCD doesn’t reveal your character. Instead, it attacks your values.

Could I be dealing with OCD?

If you’ve been reading this article and wondering whether this could apply to you, here are some common symptoms of OCD.

OCD may be the culprit if you:

  • Experience recurring intrusive thoughts, images, or urges that feel unwanted and distressing.
  • Spend a significant amount of time trying to figure out what your thoughts mean.
  • Constantly seek reassurance from others that everything is okay.
  • Feel driven to check, repeat, confess, avoid, or perform mental rituals to reduce anxiety.
  • Feel temporary relief after completing a compulsion, only to have the fear return later.
  • Find yourself avoiding people, places, objects, or situations that trigger intrusive thoughts.
  • Spend an hour or more each day consumed by obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors.
  • Notice that the anxiety is interfering with your work, relationships, parenting, school, or ability to enjoy life.

It is important to remember that everyone experiences intrusive thoughts from time to time. Having an intrusive thought does not necessarily mean you are dealing with OCD. The difference is how your brain responds to the thought. For someone who isn’t fighting OCD, the thought usually comes and goes without much attention.

For someone who is facing OCD, the thought can become “sticky.” The brain treats it like an emergency that must be solved immediately. This is where compulsions may develop. But, the more you try to make the thought go away, the stronger it often becomes. This only makes the cycles stronger.

If this cycle sounds familiar, know that you are not alone. OCD affects millions of people, and many go years before receiving an accurate diagnosis because they don’t realize what they’re experiencing has a name.

There is hope

If you recognized yourself in this article, know that OCD is highly treatable. You do not have to stay trapped in the exhausting cycle of obsessions (sticky thoughts) and/or compulsions (behaviors you adopt to relieve the anxiety you feel).

Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a specialized form of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), is the gold-standard treatment for OCD. Rather than trying to eliminate intrusive thoughts, ERP helps you change your response to them so they gradually lose their power.

Recovery doesn’t mean you’ll never have another intrusive thought. It means those thoughts no longer control your life.

If you’re struggling with OCD or intrusive thoughts, I’d love to help. Reach out today to schedule an appointment and learn how evidence-based treatment can help you break free from OCD and regain peace.
